# Pragmatism Is the Empiricist Attitude in a More Radical Form

Pragmatism represents a perfectly familiar attitude in philosophy, the empiricist attitude, but it represents it,[^1] both in a more radical and in a less objectionable form than it has ever yet assumed.[^2] A pragmatist turns his back resolutely and once for all upon a lot of inveterate habits dear to professional philosophers.[^3] He turns away from abstraction and insufficiency, from verbal solutions, from bad a priori reasons, from fixed principles, closed systems, and pretended absolutes and origins.[^4] He turns towards concreteness and adequacy, towards facts, towards action, and towards power.[^5] That means the empiricist temper regnant, and the rationalist temper sincerely given up.[^6] It means the open air and possibilities of nature, as against dogma, artificiality and the pretence of finality in truth.[^7]
